body:
Figure 1 shows the wall of a **vein**.

1. Assign specific names to the parts labelled **A–E**.
2. Mention the layer of elastic fibres in arteries which is absent in the diagram.
3. How are the cells in this vessel nourished?

media.caption: Section of the wall of a vein: A on the innermost flat cell layer, B on spindle-shaped red cells in the middle and outer layers, brackets C (thin inner layer), D (middle muscular layer) and E (thick outer layer).

answer:
1. | Label | Part |
   |---|---|
   | **A** | Endothelium |
   | **B** | Smooth muscle (cells) |
   | **C** | Tunica intima |
   | **D** | Tunica media |
   | **E** | Tunica externa (adventitia) |
2. The **internal elastic lamina** (and the **external elastic lamina**): well-developed sheets of elastic fibres in arteries that are absent or indistinct in veins.
3. The inner layers (endothelium, inner media) are nourished by **diffusion from the blood in the lumen**; the outer wall is supplied by the **vasa vasorum** (small vessels in the tunica externa). Because venous blood is poor in oxygen, vasa vasorum in veins penetrate deeper, often close to the intima.

> [!answer]
> A endothelium, B smooth muscle, C tunica intima, D tunica media, E tunica externa; internal (and external) elastic lamina; by diffusion from the lumen and by the vasa vasorum.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Vessel walls have three tunics. Veins have a thin media with little smooth muscle and elastic tissue, a thick collagenous externa (which may contain longitudinal smooth muscle) and no distinct elastic laminae, so they are thin-walled, collapse when empty and act as capacitance (blood reservoir) vessels.

## Simplified explanation

The vein wall has a lining (endothelium, intima), a muscle layer (media) and an outer coat (externa). Arteries have elastic sheets that veins lack. The wall is fed from the blood inside and by tiny vessels in its outer coat (vasa vasorum).

body:
Figure 2 shows a capillary bed between an arteriole and a venule.

1. Label the parts labelled **A–E**.
2. Describe how the **precapillary sphincter** regulates blood flow in the capillary network.

media.caption: Capillary bed: an arteriole (red, top left) and a venule (blue, top right). A points to the central channel crossing the bed, B to the small branching vessels, C to a ring where a small vessel leaves the arterial side, D to a vessel looping along the bottom directly from the arterial side to the venous side, E to the blue vessel collecting blood into the venule.

answer:
1. | Label | Part |
   |---|---|
   | **A** | Metarteriole (continuing as the thoroughfare channel) |
   | **B** | (True) capillaries |
   | **C** | Precapillary sphincter |
   | **D** | Arteriovenous anastomosis (shunt) |
   | **E** | Small (postcapillary) venule |
2. A **precapillary sphincter** is a ring of **smooth muscle** where a true capillary leaves the metarteriole.
   - When it **contracts**, the capillary entrance closes and blood bypasses the bed through the metarteriole–thoroughfare channel (or AV anastomosis) to the venule.
   - When it **relaxes**, blood flows through the true capillaries for exchange.
   - Sphincters open and close rhythmically (**vasomotion**) and respond mainly to **local factors**: low O₂, high CO₂, H⁺, lactate, adenosine, K⁺, NO and raised temperature cause relaxation (more flow to active tissue); also to sympathetic stimulation and hormones.

> [!answer]
> A metarteriole/thoroughfare channel, B capillaries, C precapillary sphincter, D arteriovenous anastomosis, E small venule. The smooth-muscle sphincter contracts to shut blood out of the capillaries (diverting it through the shunt) and relaxes to let blood in, mainly under local metabolic control.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

This is **autoregulation** of capillary perfusion: at rest only about a quarter of capillaries in skeletal muscle are open; during activity accumulated metabolites relax the sphincters and recruit more capillaries, increasing surface area for exchange.

## Simplified explanation

Little muscle rings (precapillary sphincters) act like gates: shut, blood takes the shortcut; open, blood flows through the capillaries. They open when the tissue needs more oxygen.
hint: Think of a gate at the start of each capillary.

body: Figure 4 shows the rectum and anus. Explain how the structure labelled **D** controls defecation.

media.caption: Coronal section of the rectum and anal canal: A and B point into the anal canal lining, C to the inner smooth muscle ring around the canal, D to the outer red striated muscle ring, E to the anal opening.

answer:
**D** is the **external anal sphincter**.

- It is a ring of **skeletal (striated) muscle**, under **voluntary control** via the **pudendal nerve** (S2–S4).
- When faeces distend the rectum, stretch receptors trigger the **defecation reflex**: the rectum contracts and the **internal anal sphincter** (smooth muscle, involuntary) relaxes.
- The person then decides: if it is inconvenient, the external sphincter is **kept contracted** and defecation is postponed (the reflex fades and the rectum relaxes); if appropriate, the external sphincter is **voluntarily relaxed**, aided by straining (Valsalva: closed glottis, contraction of abdominal muscles and diaphragm), and faeces are expelled.

> [!answer]
> D is the external anal sphincter: voluntary skeletal muscle (pudendal nerve) that stays contracted to hold back faeces and is consciously relaxed to allow defecation once the reflex has relaxed the internal sphincter.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Continence depends on both sphincters plus the puborectalis sling. The internal sphincter (C) gives resting tone and is controlled by the autonomic system; the external sphincter adds voluntary control learned during toilet training. Damage to the pudendal nerve or spinal cord can cause faecal incontinence.

## Simplified explanation

D is the outer ring of muscle you can control. You squeeze it to wait and relax it when you choose to go.

body:
Figure 6 shows the ovarian cycle (follicles and other structures labelled A–F around the ovary).

1. What hormone(s) is/are produced by **E**?
2. Which label indicates ovulation has taken place?

media.caption: Ovary showing stages of the ovarian cycle: C a tiny primordial follicle, B small growing follicles, A a large follicle, D a red mottled body, E a yellow body, F a large follicle bursting at the surface beside the uterine tube.

answer:
1. **E** is the **corpus luteum** (yellow body). It secretes mainly **progesterone**, together with **oestrogen** (and inhibin).
2. **F**: the mature follicle has ruptured at the ovarian surface and released the secondary oocyte (ovulation).

> [!answer]
> E (corpus luteum): progesterone and oestrogen. F indicates ovulation.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

After ovulation the remaining granulosa and theca cells, under LH, form the **corpus luteum**, which prepares and maintains the endometrium (secretory phase). Without fertilisation it degenerates after about 10–14 days into the **corpus albicans**; with pregnancy, hCG keeps it active until the placenta takes over.

## Simplified explanation

The yellow body left after an egg is released makes progesterone and oestrogen. F shows the follicle bursting to release the egg.
